title: Rioja
description: Spain's most famous region: Tempranillo, oak and an ageing system written into law.
L: Rioja lies in northern Spain, along the Ebro river and its tributaries, including the small Oja river that may give Rioja its name. It spans three regions: La Rioja, the Basque Country, Álava, and Navarra. Vineyards cover about 66,000 hectares, from about 300 to over 700 m. The Sierra de Cantabria shelters it from the north.

Rioja sits where Atlantic and Mediterranean influences meet. The west is cooler and wetter, with Atlantic air; the east is warmer and drier, Mediterranean. The Sierra de Cantabria blocks cold, wet winds from the Bay of Biscay. This range of climates lets growers blend grapes from different areas for balance.
What shelters Rioja from cold northern winds?
The mountains block Atlantic winds from the north.

In the 1860s and 1870s, when phylloxera and mildew ruined Bordeaux, French merchants came to Rioja looking for wine. They brought Bordeaux techniques, like ageing in small oak barrels, and the railway linked Rioja to France. Houses like Marqués de Riscal, 1858, and Marqués de Murrieta founded modern Rioja. Rioja became Spain's first DOCa in 1991.
French merchants brought barrel ageing to Rioja in the 19th century.
Rioja follows the Ebro across three regions
Atlantic and Mediterranean influences meet there
Bordeaux merchants shaped modern Rioja; DOCa since 1991

Tempranillo covers about 88% of Rioja's red vineyards: red cherry, strawberry, leather and tobacco, with moderate acidity. Garnacha adds body, alcohol and red fruit, especially in the warmer east. Graciano adds acidity, colour and aroma, but is low-yielding. Mazuelo, Carignan, adds acidity and tannin. Maturana Tinta is a revived native.

White Rioja is mainly Viura, Macabeo elsewhere, with Malvasía and Garnacha Blanca, and since 2007, some Tempranillo Blanco, Verdejo and others. Traditional white Rioja is aged long in oak, nutty and oxidative, as at López de Heredia. Rioja also makes rosado, mostly from Garnacha and Tempranillo.
Match each grape to its role.
Traditional white Rioja, aged for years in oak, is one of Spain's most distinctive wines, nutty and complex.
What share of Rioja's red vineyards is Tempranillo?
Tempranillo is about 88% of Rioja's reds
Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo add body, acidity and colour
Explain the role of American oak

Rioja's categories set minimum ageing for reds. Crianza: two years, at least one in barrel. Reserva: three years, at least one in barrel and six months in bottle. Gran Reserva: five years, at least two in barrel and two in bottle. Joven or Genérico wines have little or no barrel age. A coloured seal on the back label shows the category.

Rioja's barrels are traditionally 225-litre barricas of American oak, giving vanilla, coconut and dill. Long ageing in old oak gives traditional Rioja its pale colour, mellow fruit and leather. Since the 1990s, many producers use French oak and shorter ageing for darker, fruitier wines. Both styles thrive.
Order Rioja's categories by minimum ageing, shortest first.
Each category requires more time in barrel and bottle.

Each bottle carries a back-label seal from the Consejo Regulador: green for Crianza, burgundy red for Reserva, blue for Gran Reserva, and white or no barrel indication for Genérico. This makes the category easy to spot even if the front label doesn't say it.
What does American oak typically give Rioja?
American oak's lactones give these notes.
Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva set minimum ageing
American oak gives vanilla and coconut; French oak is now common

Rioja Alta, in the west, south of the Ebro, is higher, cooler and Atlantic-influenced, with clay-limestone, ferrous clay and alluvial soils; Haro is its historic centre. Rioja Alavesa, north of the Ebro, in the Basque Country, has chalky clay-limestone on terraces. Both give elegant, fresh, structured Tempranillo.
Alta and Alavesa: cool and elegant

Rioja Oriental, formerly Rioja Baja, renamed in 2018, is the eastern zone, lower, warmer and drier, Mediterranean. Alluvial and clay soils suit Garnacha, which thrives there. Wines are riper and fuller. Since 2017, labels can name the zone, and from 2018 municipalities, if the grapes come from there.
Match each sub-zone to its feature.
Each zone gives Rioja a different character.

Traditionally, Rioja houses blended grapes from all three zones for balance and consistency. Today, more producers make wines from a single zone, village or vineyard, showing place. This shift from house style to terroir is the biggest change in modern Rioja.
Rioja Oriental was formerly called Rioja Baja.
Rioja Alta and Alavesa are cool and elegant
Rioja Oriental is warm and suits Garnacha
Rioja is moving from blends to place-specific wines
Name key producers of the movement

In 2017, Rioja created Viñedo Singular, single vineyard, for wines from specific, registered plots. Rules include vines at least 35 years old, low yields, hand harvesting and tasting approval. It aims to recognise the best sites, as in Burgundy. Labels can also name a village, Vino de Municipio, or a zone, Vino de Zona.

For a century, Rioja focused on ageing and blending, not site. Producers like Remírez de Ganuza, Artadi, Contino and Telmo Rodríguez pushed for place-based classification. Some, like Artadi, left the DOCa in 2015 in protest before the new rules. The debate continues about how far Rioja should go towards a Burgundian model.
Which is a requirement for Viñedo Singular?
Old vines, low yields and hand harvesting are required.

Some historic Rioja wines were single vineyard long before the rules: Viña Tondonia, from López de Heredia, since 1913; Contino, the first single-estate Rioja in the 1970s. These show that site has always mattered, even under the blending tradition.
Which are Rioja's place-based label categories?
Viñedo Singular, since 2017, names single vineyards
Village and zone wines show place
Historic wines like Viña Tondonia were early single vineyards
Reading Rioja and eating with it

Rioja labels show the producer, the vintage, the category, Crianza, Reserva or Gran Reserva, and sometimes the zone, village or Viñedo Singular. The back label carries the Consejo Regulador seal. Cosecha or Genérico wines don't follow the ageing ladder and may be young or modern.

Rioja suits lamb, especially chuletillas, small lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings; roast suckling pig; chorizo; jamón ibérico; and Manchego. Gran Reserva suits mushrooms, game and stews. Crianza suits tapas. White Rioja suits fish and oxidative styles suit aged cheese.
Which dish is a Rioja classic?
Lamb chops grilled over vine cuttings
An old Gran Reserva may throw sediment. Stand it up for a day and decant gently; its pale colour is normal.
A pale, garnet colour in old Gran Reserva is a fault.
Not true. Long oak and bottle ageing naturally lighten the colour.
Labels show category, seal and sometimes place
Rioja suits lamb, jamón and Manchego
Old Gran Reservas are pale, mellow and best decanted gently

Rioja follows the Ebro, between Atlantic and Mediterranean
